items.title: Threats from Iran have increased substantially, US intelligence director says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Threats from Iran to Americans inside and outside the United States have increased substantially, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers on Wednesday.

"We remain committed to detecting, deterring, and combating the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton said at a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing.

"These threats have substantially increased. Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat."

Iran has warned that it would attack American forces and regional allies in retaliation for US strikes on the country, which continue more than eight months after the US and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran in February.

In a memo seen last month by Reuters, Clayton said Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, and lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached "advanced stages."

A CNN report this week cited US intelligence assessments on the possibility that Iran may be planning an attack involving a dirty bomb in Washington.

Asked about the report during Wednesday's hearing, Clayton said he would not discuss any specific matters but acknowledged such threats were not new.

"There are a suite of threats that are that we refer to as, you know, civilian mass destruction threats or whatever you want, and they have been around for a long time," Clayton said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday he did not think there was any imminent threat to the US capital, when asked about the report during a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump.

Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack.

items.title: Transportation Secretary Duffy says US taking steps to avoid future aviation disruptions
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Wednesday a problem with a router that led to a nationwide aviation ground stop should have been identified faster and officials are taking steps to prevent future disruptions.

"There's a lot of lessons that have been learned, performance lessons from some of our contractors that we are thoroughly addressing right now," Duffy said during an appearance on the online podcast "The Morning Meeting."

Duffy has said a Juniper router installed by L3Harris Technologies (LHX.N) in a remote Arkansas facility triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide aviation ground stop on Friday, the longest in the United States since the September 11, 2001, attacks.

"The team you have monitoring the network to see any issue and isolate that issue and remove it from the network -- that is critical when you do this work," Duffy said. "This was not identified quick enough. It was not isolated quick enough. We're working on how to remedy that right now."

L3Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Duffy said the installation of 68 prior routers, which are made by Hewlett Packard Enterprise-owned (HPE.N) Juniper Networks, had not led to any problems. But he said the Federal Aviation Administration has paused installations of Juniper routers as testing continues at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida with the FAA, Cisco (CSCO.O) and the FBI on site.

Duffy has asked Congress to quickly approve another $50 billion to complete massive upgrades in the aging US air traffic control system and airports after lawmakers last year approved $12.5 billion. Some lawmakers support a smaller amount of money targeted at the safety upgrades.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford took responsibility for the ground stop that disrupted the travel plans of 1 million travelers.

"I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it," Bedford said at a forum with the Hill newspaper. "I've been hired to get this done. So blame me if we need to blame somebody. Blame me."

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: Democrats probe whether Lutnick helped Cantor Fitzgerald avoid Nvidia-linked losses
items.content_html:
Nov 18 (Reuters) - Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into whether US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick used his office to help investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald, which is controlled by his sons, avoid losses linked to the scandal at AI chip firm Nvidia (NVDA.O), according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

In the letter dated November 17, House Democrats notified Brandon Lutnick, chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald and Howard Lutnick's son, that they are requesting information to ascertain if any actions taken by the commerce secretary were "improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald's holdings or business interests."

The lawmakers — Jamie Raskin, Gregory Meeks and Sydney Kamlager-Dove — asked if concerns about Cantor Fitzgerald's "financial exposure, business relationships, or contracts with or commitments to foreign governments" influenced Secretary Lutnick's refusal to add Megaspeed to its trade blacklist for certain technology or require a license for the export of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed.

The US puts companies on its trade blacklist that it has determined pose risks to US national security or foreign policy.

"The Secretary has fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including all divestiture and recusal requirements, and will continue to do so. He has divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, Newmark, and BGC," a Commerce spokesperson said in a statement in response to the letter, which was first reported by The Financial Times.

Megaspeed has been in the spotlight after reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy.

Cantor Fitzgerald denied the claims, saying in an emailed statement it holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia, and that its Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients. The firm also said it has no role in US export control or blacklist decisions.

Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four government agencies had favored putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist but the Commerce Department, which was in charge, had not.

Reuters has also reported that senior White House officials have discussed whether Lutnick should be pushed out.

items.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for next US House speaker
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Democrats elected this month to the US House of Representatives nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to lead them in the next Congress, putting him on the precipice of becoming the nation's first Black House speaker.

The incoming House Democratic Caucus nominated Jeffries in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote. Jeffries won 251 votes with 11 Democrats opposing him.

Many incoming progressives declined to say whether they would back Jeffries after the November 3 midterm elections, with several saying they wanted a leader who would support a bold agenda to pass populist policies that candidates campaigned on.

A group of seven incoming House progressives said in a joint statement that they voted against Jeffries because they're still working to secure commitments from the New York Democrat.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership," they said. "Those conversations are ongoing."

DEMOCRATS MINIMIZE INTERNAL DIVISIONS

Leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus congratulated Jeffries in a separate statement that pledged to work with him to pass "the first year of Medicare For All, an end to for-profit immigrant detention centers, and so much more."

Representative Pramila Jayapal, a former chair of the progressive group who voted for Jeffries, said it's legitimate for new members to "want to respond to the anger of the moment that's out there, and I think Leader Jeffries — soon-to-be Speaker Jeffries — understands that, in part because the movement has been so effective at communicating that."

Other Democrats downplayed the significance of the opposition. Representative Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, told reporters there will always be naysayers, and Representative Jonathan Jackson said Democrats "can have a majority without being a monopoly."

"Rarely are great people able to reach their ultimate goal without somebody saying no," Representative Emanuel Cleaver told Reuters. "It just doesn't happen."

Despite some opposition, Jeffries is expected to be elected speaker, a powerful position that puts him second in line to the presidency, when the new Congress convenes in early January. The speaker election requires 218 votes on the House floor. Democrats will have a majority of at least 257 seats. Several competitive races remain uncalled.

HISTORIC MILESTONE CELEBRATED

Several Democrats celebrated the historic nature of Jeffries' nomination. Representative Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, who was the highest-ranking Black House Democrat until Jeffries became Democratic leader, told reporters that Wednesday's vote was "very historic."

Representative Joe Morelle, a fellow New York Democrat, said he was overjoyed for Jeffries, someone he's known for nearly two decades.

"He's going to be a great speaker," he told Reuters.

Asked about the members Jeffries has yet to win over, Morelle said there was broad consensus in the caucus on advancing an affordability and accountability agenda that Democrats campaigned on.

"I'm sure there'll be other voices," he said. "But I think he is focused on delivering on what we talked about this fall."

Representative Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania framed the vote as a continuation of the "bright turnaround" Democrats have experienced since Election Day.

"I didn't allow myself to dream of this sweeping set of wins," she said, referring to Democrats winning control of the House and Senate. "And yet here we are on a much brighter day, with an extraordinarily capable leadership team that will serve for the American people."

House Republicans last week nominated Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to lead their conference in January. Jordan won the post over Majority Leader Steve Scalise after Speaker Mike Johnson said he would not seek to lead Republicans in the minority.

items.title: US single-family housing starts rebound in October; building permits plunge
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - US single-family homebuilding rebounded in October, but the improvement is likely temporary, with permits for future construction dropping to their lowest level in over 3-1/2 years as high mortgage rates continued to depress housing demand.

The housing market has been in a slump since mid-2024, a downturn exacerbated by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which is fanning inflation and driving up borrowing costs, leaving many young Americans unable to afford buying a home. Economists expect the housing market downturn to persist in 2027, especially with the Federal Reserve forecast to continue raising interest rates after next month's widely expected hike to quell inflation.

The report from the Commerce Department on Wednesday followed on the heels of a survey this week showing sentiment among single-family homebuilders diving to a more than 14-1/2-year low in November.

"Homebuilding remains in the doldrums, with elevated borrowing costs hurting developers by squeezing demand while significantly raising the cost of construction," said Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics.

Single-family housing starts, which account for the bulk of homebuilding, increased 4.0% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 864,000 units last month, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau said. Building permits for single-family housing projects tumbled 8.7% to a rate of 772,000 units, the lowest level since January 2023. Building permits fell in all four regions, with a double-digit decline in the West.

The rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage has surged by 120 basis points since the conflict started in late February, data from mortgage finance agency Freddie Mac showed, averaging 7.18% last week. Financial markets have priced in a 25-basis-point rate hike at the US central bank's December 8-9 meeting and anticipated another increase in borrowing costs in January, CME's FedWatch tool showed.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Wednesday the central bank needs to get more aggressive in its response to inflation that he fears is changing public psychology about prices, and either approve a half-point hike at the December meeting or communicate a faster pace of hikes in 2027.

The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month.

In addition to elevated mortgage rates suppressing housing demand, homebuilding is also being constrained by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, which the National Association of Home Builders said on Tuesday was "keeping legal workers off construction sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs." Developers were also facing growing cost pressures from high energy and material prices.

An overhang of unsold new homes on the market is also constraining single-family homebuilding.

Residential investment, which includes homebuilding, has contracted in eight of the last 10 quarters. The housing market drag has not dented the economy as it accounts for a small share of gross domestic product.

Starts for housing projects with five units or more, a very volatile segment, soared 25.5% to a rate of 433,000 units in October. Multifamily housing starts increased 22.0% on a year-over-year basis. Overall housing starts rebounded 9.9% to a pace of 1.309 million units. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast starts rising to a rate of 1.245 million units.

They rose 2.8% on a year-over-year basis in October.

Building permits for multifamily housing projects fell 5.2% to a rate of 475,000 units last month. Overall building permits tumbled 7.4% to a rate of 1.295 million units. Economists had forecast permits rising to a rate of 1.377 million units.

Permits declined 8.7% on a year-over-year basis in October.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Andrea Ricci

items.title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins in Alaska, securing 56-44 US Senate majority
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Democrat Mary Peltola won Alaska's US Senate race on Tuesday, projections from US media showed, defeating Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and giving her party its ninth Senate flip of the midterm elections and a commanding 56-44 majority in the upper house of Congress.

Peltola, 53, who made a living in the commercial fishing industry before entering politics, also becomes the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in her home state in nearly 20 years and the first Alaska Native ever to do so.

Alaska Natives account for roughly 15% to 18% of Alaska's population, the highest Indigenous proportion of any US state.

The contest was the final uncalled midterm race in the Senate. Peltola's win gives Democrats their largest Senate majority since 2009 which, combined with securing control over the House of Representatives, sets up two years of possible deadlock between Congress and Republican President Donald Trump.

Peltola was projected to have won 50% of first-place votes to Sullivan's 46%, enough to clear the 50% threshold and avoid additional rounds under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system.

Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but voter frustration with the high cost of living and the state's strong independent political streak put it back in play for Democrats.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said on X after media projected her victory. "Thank you, Alaska. Let's get to work."

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who enlisted Peltola to challenge Sullivan, hailed her victory in a separate message posted on X as a "gift to Alaska, the Senate, and all of America."

'FISH, FAMILY AND FREEDOM'

"It's official: 56 Democratic Senate seats!" Schumer wrote. "Her knowledge and love for Alaska are unparalleled, and she ran a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about – fish, family, and freedom."

Alaska's far-flung and isolated communities can make its election counts unusually lengthy. The race was further complicated by allegations that Democrats helped recruit an independent candidate as a spoiler.

Two other candidates were on the general-election ballot: Republican Gerry Heikes, a drywall contractor, and Dan J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher running as an independent.

Republicans alleged that Sullivan Jr. was recruited to confuse voters who supported the incumbent senator and unsuccessfully sought to remove him from the ballot, arguing he was not a "good faith" candidate. Alaska's Supreme Court rejected that argument.

Just before Election Day, the New York Times reported that Peltola's campaign had helped recruit Sullivan Jr. into the race. Peltola's campaign denied any involvement. Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation into the allegations and has said it was examining anything that could "resemble perjury."

The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation into possible wrongdoing. US Attorney General Todd Blanche has described the reported recruitment effort as "fraud."

The department has sent more than 140 subpoenas, letters and notices in its investigation, Reuters previously reported, though those actions do not indicate guilt.

Peltola became the first Alaska Native ever elected to Congress in 2022 in a special election to fill Alaska's lone House seat following the death of longtime Republican incumbent Don Young.

In that race, she defeated two brand-name Alaska Republicans in an upset victory over former Governor Sarah Palin and Nick Begich III, helped by the endorsement of Alaska Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski and Young's congressional staff. She was re-elected to a full two-year term in 2022, but lost her bid for a second full term in 2024 to Begich.

Born in Anchorage, Peltola grew up in several communities along the Kuskokwim River in southwestern Alaska. Her mother was a member of the Yup'ik group of Alaska Natives and her father was a German American who moved to Alaska from Nebraska.

Reporting by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff, Jason Lange, Dan Catchpole and Steve Gorman; Editing by Michael Learmonth, Howard Goller, Lincoln Feast and Stephen Coates

items.title: Five takeaways from Trump's Asia tour: cabinet feuds, Rubio love and a Kim Jong Un curveball
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump is in Asia this week for talks with foreign leaders in Manila, followed by a visit to China to meet President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and possibly the elusive North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Here are some takeaways from Trump's journey so far.

TROUBLES FROM HOME FOLLOW TRUMP ABROAD

Trump may be thousands of miles from Washington, but a string of disruptions back home has followed him to Asia.

National outages affecting flights, online banking, Microsoft and other services have unsettled some of Trump's allies and prompted Republicans in Congress to call for the administration to brief lawmakers.

“I’m checking my bank account with a little bit of worry,” former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said on “Fox & Friends” on Tuesday, urging the White House to be transparent.

Vice President JD Vance said he had heard similar worries.

“I’ve had a lot of my friends reach out and say, ‘Should we be preparing to build a bunker and stock up on food and water?’ and my answer to that is no, we do not see some crisis coming down but you have to be prepared for everything,” Vance told Fox News’ “The Ingraham Angle” on Monday.

Trump, speaking to reporters in the Philippines on Tuesday, brushed aside concerns about the outages.

“It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine,” the president said, standing beside the leaders of Japan, Australia and India. “It's going to be very much under control.”

BESSENT VS LUTNICK, WITH TRUMP AS REFEREE

A feud inside Trump's cabinet also followed him to Asia, putting two competing approaches to China side by side as the president prepares for one of the trip's most consequential meetings.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is at odds with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a visible strain within a second-term Trump team that has largely avoided the infighting that marked his first term.

Bessent has said he is unhappy with Lutnick for stalling Trump's crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's (NVDA.O) chips to China.

Lutnick has cautioned he wants to avoid reigniting a trade war with Beijing over the issue, which has drawn renewed scrutiny since revelations about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Bessent and Lutnick flew together on Air Force One to Manila as TVs on the plane played up tensions within the cabinet. The two men avoided eye contact when they sat next to each other at a meeting in Manila.

Trump, for now, seems to have taken a let-them-fight-it-out attitude.

“One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China. They both are acceptable, but they are different views,” Trump told reporters on Monday as he departed the White House, adding later: “I'll make a decision.”

HARRY HOUDINI MAKES AN APPEARANCE ON AIR FORCE ONE

Add Harry Houdini to the list of unexpected cameos in Trump's Asia tour.

Reporters on Air Force One are used to having their TV screens on the plane locked on the president's favorite network, the Fox News Channel, nearly all the time, with Trump in command of the remote control.

But during the 18-hour flight to Manila, the screens abruptly switched to a Fox Nation documentary about Houdini, the Hungarian-born escape artist, complete with AI-generated images. Houdini died in 1926 and is buried in Trump's native Queens, New York.

After the detour into the television drama, the cabin TVs went back to Fox News and Laura Ingraham's interview with Vance.

TRUMP PRAISES RUBIO

Trump doesn't appear ready to anoint a 2028 successor, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio keeps getting conspicuous praise from the president.

The attention has added intrigue to the question of whether he could eventually favor Rubio over Vance in the Republican nominating race. Trump has noted a lot of Republicans will probably run and at times has queried Oval Office visitors on whether they prefer “JD or Marco?”

Neither man has announced plans to run, although the Vance team has said he is considering it.

Rubio, a former US senator from Florida, has been coy about his plans for 2028. Some people in his orbit say he does not want to run against Vance and may choose to enter the private sector before considering a run in 2032.

Trump has repeatedly highlighted Rubio's political appeal, including the cheers he received when Trump brought him on stage at campaign rallies before the midterm elections.

In Manila, Trump joked that he would fire Rubio if he did not respond to calls from regional leaders in the room, but then he turned up the praise.

“How hot is Marco, right? Is Marco doing a great job? He's been fantastic,” said Trump.

At the ASEAN dinner Tuesday night, Rubio sat directly across the table from Trump.

A KIM JONG UN CURVEBALL

Trump's planned talks with Xi and Putin in China are expected to be the centerpiece of his Asia trip.

But as he left the White House on Monday, Trump dangled the prospect that he might also meet with North Korea's Kim on the final stop.

In his first term, Trump had three high-profile summits with Kim that were long on optics but short on addressing North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons power. Trump has tried to renew personal diplomacy in his second term with no success.

So far there has been no sign Kim plans to make the trip. As Trump prepared for Thursday's trilateral summit with Xi and Putin, Kim was seen at a ski resort near the Chinese border.

Reporting by Trevor Hunnicutt, Bo Erickson and Steve Holland; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: US Democratic senator introduces bill to end China's trade status ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - US Democratic Senator Tammy Baldwin on Tuesday introduced legislation to revoke China's normal trade status and favorable tariff treatment just days before US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to meet for a third time this year to discuss a delicate trade truce.

Baldwin's bill, which argues that Beijing had failed to uphold the principles of fair trade, would set a deadline to end the permanent normal trade relations that have been in effect since 2002 a year after the legislation is enacted.

The legislation, which could have more support under a Congress controlled by Democrats next year, would shift Chinese imports to higher regular US tariff rates under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule.

The existing US "Most Favored Nation" tariff rates for China and other countries average about 2.5%, but Trump has heaped punitive duties on Chinese imports, about 25% during his first term and up to 20% during his second term under a trade truce with Beijing.

Baldwin's bill also would direct the US Trade Representative's office to issue a report together with the Commerce Department and US International Trade Commission and other bodies on ongoing trade and economic challenges posed by China.

Lawmakers have repeatedly sought to revoke China's special treatment in recent years, but the bills have failed due to competing economic priorities, legislative bottlenecks, and shifting trade dynamics, with Republicans not challenging Trump's tariff pressure. But there is growing anti-China sentiment in Congress, particularly among Democrats who won control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in elections this month.

Trump, who meets with Xi in Shenzhen, China, this week, could still veto the bill if it passes.

"We need to reset our trade relationship with China, be honest that they have undercut us at every turn, and put the focus back where it matters — prioritizing American workers, manufacturers and families," said Baldwin, who voted against the change in China's tariff treatment in 2000 while serving in the House of Representatives.

She said in a statement that the US had "rolled out the red carpet for China" for two decades while Beijing had engaged in market manipulation, intellectual property theft and other unfair trade practices, noting that the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, an independent, bipartisan legislative agency, also recommended revoking the PNTR status of China in November 2024.

Western concerns about China's efforts to dominate global markets have grown in recent years, fueled by Beijing's threats to shut off exports of critical minerals needed for advanced manufacturing — and its actual moves to do so for Japan.

Trump, who ordered a review of China's trade status when he took office in January 2025, and Xi are expected to discuss a fragile trade-war truce that will expire in January when they meet later this week amid growing tensions over trade. China's foreign ministry has accused the US of "economic coercion" over its latest restrictions on Chinese access to advanced chips.

Baldwin's office said there was "growing recognition that granting China PNTR failed to deliver the changes in China's economic and trade practices that were promised," and the bill would establish a more durable US trade policy.

Revoking China's current trade status would increase the price of Chinese imports, especially for manufactured goods, and in the long run, raise US consumer prices by 0.7% and reduce US economic output by 0.2%, the US International Trade Commission said in a 319-page report released in August.

But two ITC commissioners — a Republican and a Democrat — challenged the notion that ending PNTR status for China would raise costs, arguing that the analysis failed to account for economic harm caused by granting it in the first place.

The ITC concluded that revoking PNTR would raise trade-weighted average tariffs by 35.2 percentage points.

Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by Andrea Ricci

items.title: At hearing, US Navy chief blasted over Iran war and its toll on sailors
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Democratic lawmakers tore into President Donald Trump's acting head of the Navy on Tuesday, accusing him of being a Trump "yes man" on the Iran war and downplaying its toll on sailors' mental health after eight suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier.

The contentious hearing during the waning days of the Republican-led Senate could be a preview of what's to come when Democrats take control in January after victories in midterm elections earlier this month.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who is seeking to win Senate confirmation to keep the job, did not directly respond to some of the toughest questions before the Senate Armed Services Committee about the Iran war. Those included the cost of the US naval blockade on Iran and the damage to the Navy's headquarters in the Middle East after attacks by Iran.

But it was his defense of Navy conditions on board the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group and his praise for the Navy's mental health crisis response that drew the fiercest criticism from Democratic senators.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York, asked him about a sailor who went overboard.

"Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself and he admitted that," Cao told her, saying he used a life preserver.

Gillibrand responded: "What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?"

"I think you are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members," Gillibrand replied, adding she thought Cao's response was "inhumane" and "inadequate."

Republican Representative Rob Wittman from Virginia extolled Cao as he introduced him as "a remarkable American story," a refugee from Vietnam who served in the Navy for 25 years, including in Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia, retiring at the rank of captain.

Cao, whose son is in the Marine Corps, told the committee he wanted the job to ensure sailors "don't go to war the way we did" in Iraq, without armored vehicles or enough body armor.

Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, said he was moved by Cao's personal story but said it was also ironic as Trump's administration cuts refugee admissions.

"Today, your family wouldn't be let in the country," King said.

QUANTITY FOR QUALITY?

Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas dismissed talk of poor conditions on Navy ships. "If the picture painted by the Democrats were so bleak, would the Navy have reached its recruiting goals three months early?" he asked.

Cao responded, "Senator, we would not be there."

Senator Jack Reed, a Democrat from Rhode Island, pointed to data he said showed most new Navy recruits required waivers from standard qualification requirements — including on issues like mental health.

"Are you sort of sacrificing quality for quantity?" Reed asked, to a denial from Cao.

Cao will himself require a waiver to be confirmed to the job, since he only retired from the Navy in 2021 — putting him below the required seven-year cooling-off period to become its civilian leader.

Voter anger over the Iran war, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published last week found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran once and for all.

The Navy has played a critical role in the war, imposing a punishing naval blockade on Iran and helping deliver strikes on Iranian territory. This week, a third aircraft carrier entered Middle East waters, though officials say it is expected to replace one of the two carriers present.

While the US military points to the heavy toll imposed on Iran's conventional military, and its ability to help escort tankers through the Strait of Hormuz past Iranian shores, the Pentagon has not yet explained how it sees the conflict ending.

Senator Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois, asked whether Cao ever stood up to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war.

"Senator, it's not within my purview to do that," Cao said.

Duckworth responded sharply: "It is within your purview!"

"This is a failure of leadership by President Trump and the unqualified yes-men he's installed, and it sounds like you want to be one of those," she said.

items.title: Root cause of US aviation shutdown not yet determined, Duffy says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Tuesday that no root cause had yet been determined for the router that failed on Friday, triggering a nationwide aviation shutdown and more than 18,000 flight cancellations.

Duffy said it remained unclear why L3Harris Technologies' (LHX.N) installation of a router in a remote El Dorado, Arkansas, facility had a big enough impact on the network to lead to a nearly five-hour aviation ground stop that affected hundreds of thousands of airline passengers.

"We've been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado, but the root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet," Duffy told reporters after a meeting with senators.

The swap was part of a routine switchover from copper wire to digital fiber to modernize equipment, and FAA head Bryan Bedford told reporters that speculation that AI was involved in the outage was unfounded.

Duffy said the installation of 68 prior routers, which are made by Hewlett Packard Enterprise-owned (HPE.N) Juniper Networks, had not led to any issues. But he said the FAA has paused installations of Juniper routers as testing continues at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida with the FAA, Cisco (CSCO.O) and the FBI on site.

L3Harris has said it is cooperating with the official investigation into what went wrong.

Duffy said that during the Biden administration, the FAA replaced 19% of its telecom network from copper to fiber and in one year the Trump administration has replaced just over 50%. "We do have to get this work done. Otherwise, staying on the old system for longer is going to mean more risk," he said.

L3Harris had been installing Juniper routers to replace Cisco routers, produced in 2001, which were supposed to have been replaced in 2006, the FAA said.

Duffy said the FAA had spent a year at its tech center testing the Juniper routers, but the installation at the Arkansas radio communications site led to an overload of a key government communications system. That destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, affecting 17 of 22 FAA en route air traffic control centers.

After the incident, the broadcasting function was also disabled on all the new routers as well as 60 other routers in the system as a precaution, the FAA said.

Juniper owner HPE said it believed its equipment was working as configured. "The FAA is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause," the company said.

Reporting by David Shepardson, Daphne Psaledakis and Christian Martinez; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Jamie Freed

items.title: US retail sales showcase underlying strength despite cost-of-living crunch
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - US retail sales increased moderately in October as households pulled back on purchases of motor vehicles and furniture, but maintained spending elsewhere, keeping the economy on solid footing at the start of the fourth quarter.

The report from the Commerce Department on Tuesday also showed upward revisions to so-called core retail sales, which exclude motor vehicles among other categories, in September.

Spending has remained resilient despite rising inflation eroding purchasing power for mostly lower- and middle-income households.

The underlying strength in retail sales, together with other data on Tuesday showing a bigger-than-expected increase in import prices last month, reinforced economists' views that the Federal Reserve would continue raising interest rates after next month's widely expected hike.

"More consumers are clearly struggling with rapidly rising prices but are not yet ready to throw in the towel," said Scott Anderson, chief US economist at BMO Capital Markets.

"Instead, consumers appear to be strategically allocating their monthly budgets to stretch their dollars into different categories every month. While under some pressure, real consumer spending is expected to perform well enough in the fourth quarter to keep the Fed focused on its inflation mandate."

Retail sales rose 0.2% last month after an unrevised 0.8% surge in September, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau said. The increase was in line with economists' expectations. Retail sales are mostly goods and are not adjusted for inflation. They gained 6.8% on a year-on-year basis in October.

The ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran is driving up inflation, outpacing wage growth. The government reported last month that income at the disposal of households after adjusting for inflation and taxes fell 0.3% in September.

Some economists said the retail sales share of consumer spending was shrinking, which they attributed to the bifurcation of the household sector, with the rising cost of living disproportionately hurting middle- and lower-income households.

"They tend to spend more of their income on physical goods, such as food and clothing, and squeezed spending power limits the potential for growth," said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING.

"High-income households have seen their wealth surge, boosting consumption, and are accounting for a growing share of total consumer spending. However, they spend more of their income on services and experiences, such as leisure, hospitality and travel, which are not included in retail sales."

The ongoing technology-led selloff could temper spending by making consumers more cautious.

Retail sales last month were held back by a 1.6% decline in receipts at auto dealers. Sales at furniture retailers fell 2.3%, while receipts at electronics and appliance stores were unchanged. There were decreases in sales at clothing retailers as well as at sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument and book stores.

But building material store sales increased 0.5%, and there were strong rises in receipts at service stations as well as health and personal care outlets. Sales at nonstore retailers jumped 1.2%, likely reflecting Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days promotion. Sales at miscellaneous store retailers, including florists and pet stores, soared 4.7%.

Receipts at food services and drinking places, the only services component in the report, rose 0.2%.

GROWTH ESTIMATES REVISED UP

Retail sales excluding automobiles, gasoline, building materials and food services increased 0.6% last month after an upwardly revised 0.5% rise in September. Economists had forecast these core retail sales, which correspond most closely with the consumer spending component of gross domestic product, advancing 0.4% after a previously reported 0.1% gain in September.

That led economists to temper their expectations for a slowdown in consumer spending this quarter after growing at a 3.8% annualized rate for two straight quarters. Economists at Goldman Sachs raised their fourth-quarter GDP growth estimate by 0.6 percentage point to a 2.4% annualized rate.

The economy grew at a 3.4% pace in the July-September quarter, fueled by both consumer spending and business investment in AI, though signs are pointing to an upgrade when the government publishes its second estimate next week.

Stocks on Wall Street fell, with the Nasdaq Composite index hitting an eight-month low. The dollar slipped against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

A separate report from the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics showed import prices increased 1.1% in October after rising by the same margin in September.

Economists had forecast import prices, which exclude tariffs, climbing 0.7%. The BLS did not publish year-over-year import price readings because last year's federal government shutdown prevented the collection of data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base. Imported inflation accelerated 8.1% in September, the largest gain in just over four years.

The government last week reported stronger-than-expected consumer prices in October as well as firmer producer inflation details. Financial markets have priced in a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December and anticipated another increase in borrowing costs in January, CME's FedWatch tool showed.

The US central bank left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. Import prices were last month driven by fuels, capital goods related to AI, motor vehicles, engines and parts as well as consumer goods.

International airfares also increased. This component goes into the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, excluding food and energy, one of the inflation measures tracked by the Fed for its 2% target.

Economists continued to believe that so-called core PCE inflation increased 0.3% for the third straight month in October. In the 12 months through October, they forecast core PCE inflation advancing 3.2% after rising 3.1% in September.

AI-related investment underpinned manufacturing, with a third report from the Fed showing factory production rising 0.3% for a second consecutive month in October. Economists expected the trend to persist despite growing backlash to data centers and regulation fears following the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in this month's midterm elections.

"Policy at the state and local level will slow and prolong, not derail, the buildout," said Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics.

"A bigger risk, though, is that with inflation stubbornly elevated and the labor market showing signs of re-acceleration, the Fed presses even harder on the brakes, uncovering vulnerabilities in the most leveraged parts of the AI ecosystem and causing a sharper pullback in AI-driven spending."

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Andrea Ricci

items.title: US official says recent tech woes not tied to cyberattacks
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - A recent series of US technology outages is not tied to cyberattacks but rather to aging computer systems that are in need of upgrades, the country's top homeland security official said on Tuesday.

Disruptions at United Airlines (UAL.O), the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft (MSFT.O) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) have raised alarm.

"Some of the technology that they're pushing out there, they're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system," Markwayne Mullin told CNBC. "But it has nothing to do with cyberattacks, and I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out."

Mullin said maybe companies needed to start telling customers before conducting a scheduled upgrade and warn them of possible disruptions for a short period of time.

"I can tell you 98% certainty this isn't a cyberattack," he added.

Mullin said that at 2:20 p.m. ET on Tuesday there would be a long-scheduled test of the emergency alert system. Radio and television broadcasters nationwide will interrupt normal programming to relay a one-minute test message.

The FAA issued a nearly five-hour ground stop on Friday that led to airlines cancelling more than 18,000 flights over three days in the longest outage since the September 11, 2001, attacks. The outage was blamed on the installation of a single router in a remote facility in Arkansas.

United said a computer problem on Monday forced a halt to many departing flights, while JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, on Monday experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug but said there was no evidence it was cyber-related.

Microsoft on Saturday said services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours. Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident and it was not aware of any malicious activity.

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Nia Williams

items.title: Trump approval holds near career low at 32%, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
• 31% of Americans support US war in Iran, poll finds
  • 34% of Democrats view Senate leader Chuck Schumer favorably, 43% unfavorably

WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's approval rating held near the lowest level of his presidency, while the leader of the Democrats in the US Senate also showed signs he was losing popularity within his party on the eve of a leadership challenge, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

The four-day poll showed 32% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in the White House, a rate that has held steady in four straight Reuters/Ipsos polls since mid-October when the president's rating was 31%, a career low.

Trump's popularity has tumbled this year as the US war with Iran has hit Americans' personal finances by pushing fuel prices sharply higher, an economic conflagration that cost Trump's Republican Party control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. Just 31% of Americans support the war in Iran, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

SOUR ON SCHUMER

The poll showed Democratic respondents divided about the party's leadership in Congress, with more viewing Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer unfavorably than viewing him favorably. The party's House leader, Hakeem Jeffries, was viewed more favorably than unfavorably within his party.

Some 34% of self-identified Democrats in the poll said they have a favorable view of Schumer, who is facing a leadership challenge from fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Some 43% of Democrats in the poll said they had an unfavorable view of Schumer, while 22% said they had never heard of him.

In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in February, 38% of Democrats said they looked on Schumer favorably and 37% viewed him unfavorably.

Van Hollen has been more forceful in criticizing Israel's war in Gaza, arguing that blocks on some weapons sales to Israel might be needed. Schumer has also criticized Israel's attacks on Gaza but has voted against limits on weapons sales to the US ally.

Israel's war in Gaza, which has leveled vast swaths of the occupied territory following deadly attacks in 2023 by Palestinian militants on Israeli civilians, has sharply divided Democrats, eroding the longstanding support for Israel within the party.

Democratic lawmakers will take control of the US Senate and House of Representatives in January.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll also found that Jeffries was better liked than Schumer, with 40% of Democrats looking on him favorably and 29% unfavorably, with 29% saying they don't know the name.

Republicans are more united around their leadership, with 75% saying they like Trump and 77% saying the same of Vice President JD Vance.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, surveyed 1,521 US adults nationwide and had a margin of error of about 3 percentage points.

items.title: United Airlines says technology outage that delayed departures has been resolved
items.content_html:
CHICAGO, Nov 16 (Reuters) - United Airlines (UAL.O) said on Monday it had resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures for about an hour, just days after a nationwide air traffic control outage caused widespread disruption to US airlines.

The disruption, which ended around 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT), highlighted how computer failures can ground flights even when aircraft and crews are ready to depart.

There was no indication that United's outage was connected to Friday's Federal Aviation Administration shutdown, which caused the longest nationwide ground stop of departing flights since the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States.

"This is not an FAA system-wide problem," US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an interview on Monday on Fox News' "Hannity" show. "I don't know what the root cause of United is," he added.

United said a technology issue that delayed flight departures had been resolved, adding that flights already airborne and those operated by United Express had been unaffected throughout.

"There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," the airline said.

An internal memo from United's pilots union, seen by Reuters, said a companywide web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications.

The memo said United had been unable to provide final aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates. Such information is essential for pilots to complete pre-departure calculations.

In a subsequent memo, the union said United's systems were coming back online and directed pilots to check updated company communications.

Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday's outage involved United's Unimatic system.

Alaska Airlines (ALK.N) also briefly halted departures nationwide in April 2024 after a problem with its weight-and-balance system.

FLIGHT DISRUPTIONS

As of 6:50 p.m. ET (2350 GMT), United had delayed 645 flights, or 20% of its schedule, and canceled 25 on Monday, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. It was unclear how many of those disruptions were caused by Monday's technology issue, as airlines were still recovering from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop.

United shares went down 2.5% in after-hours trading.

Some passengers reported on social media that their aircraft had returned to the gate after reaching the runway.

The outage came as US air travel was largely returning to normal following Friday's nationwide ground stop, which lasted nearly five hours after a failure in the FAA's telecommunications network.

More than 18,100 flights scheduled to depart US airports between Friday and Sunday were canceled or had not taken off within three hours of their scheduled departure times, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. Not all were necessarily affected by the FAA outage.

items.title: US Supreme Court sidesteps fight over Maryland's 'sensitive places' gun curbs
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Monday to decide whether a Maryland law banning the carry of guns in certain "sensitive places" such as stadiums, bars and public parks violates constitutional gun rights.

The justices turned away an appeal by gun rights advocates of a lower court's decision finding that the restrictions comport with the US Constitution's Second Amendment right to "keep and bear arms."

Maryland was one of several states to enact new restrictions on the carrying of firearms in locations deemed "sensitive" after a landmark Supreme Court ruling in 2022 expanded gun rights.

Maryland's law, signed in 2023 by Democratic Governor Wes Moore, prohibited guns in such locations as college campuses, hospitals, power plants, amusement parks and places that sell alcohol or cannabis for on-site consumption. These built on Maryland's longstanding gun-carry restrictions in locations that include public transit, casinos, schools and public protest sites.

THE BRUEN TEST

Gun rights groups, including the Second Amendment Foundation, and several firearms-owning residents sued to challenge the law. They argued that a number of the state's location-based restrictions violated their Second Amendment rights as defined by the Supreme Court's 2022 decision in the case New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen.

The Bruen ruling declared for the first time that the Second Amendment protects an individual's right to carry a handgun in public for self-defense. It was one of three key rulings by the Supreme Court since 2008 that broadened gun rights in a nation deeply divided over how to address firearms violence including frequent mass shootings. The United States has the world's highest gun ownership rate.

Under a legal test set out in the Bruen decision, gun control measures must be "consistent with this nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" — not simply advance an important government interest — in order to comply with the Second Amendment. The challengers in the Maryland case argued that the state's restrictions failed the Bruen test.

A federal judge in 2023 upheld some location-based restrictions while blocking others, prompting separate appeals by gun rights groups challenging the law and Maryland officials defending it. On appeal, the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals approved all of Maryland's disputed location bans. This led to the current appeal to the Supreme Court.

JUSTICE THOMAS WEIGHS IN

Conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, who authored the Bruen ruling, in a statement attached to Monday's order said he was skeptical that Maryland's restrictions are lawful. But Thomas agreed with the decision to turn away the case, saying the broad challenge by the plaintiffs would complicate the court's review.

"In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of states' authority to ban firearms in 'sensitive places,'" Thomas wrote.

The Second Amendment Foundation expressed disappointment but noted that its challenge to New York's firearm restrictions in public parks is also pending before the court.

"We are hopeful the court takes a very hard look at that case and elects to restore the right to carry for the Americans all over the country that are subject to these unconstitutional laws," foundation official Bill Sack said.

The court further expanded gun rights in a pair of decisions this year. In a 6-3 ruling powered by its conservative majority, the court in June struck down a Hawaii law that required gun owners to get an owner's permission before bringing a handgun onto private property open to the public, such as most businesses.

The justices also decided unanimously in June to limit the application of a decades-old federal law that bars firearms possession by certain drug users, narrowing a measure that had threatened the gun rights of millions of Americans who use marijuana and own firearms.

The decisions reinforced the Bruen test that gun control measures must clear in order to survive scrutiny under the amendment, ratified in 1791. The provision states, "A well regulated militia, being necessary to the security of a free state, the right of the people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed."

The court on December 2 will hear a challenge to the legality of state restrictions on assault-style rifles, giving the justices another chance to expand gun rights in a case that involves a type of weapon often associated with mass shootings.

Reporting by John Kruzel; Additional reporting by Andrew Chung; Editing by Will Dunham

items.title: US must intensify vaccination effort to regain measles-free status lost after 26 years
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON/CHICAGO, Nov 16 (Reuters) - Public health experts say the US must drive vaccinations and disease surveillance in order to regain the hard-won measles-free status it held for 26 years that a Trump administration official said on Monday had been revoked.

The Pan American Health Organization told the Trump administration in a letter on Friday that the United States had lost the status, the official said. PAHO is expected to make the formal announcement on Tuesday.

The decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades.

About 7,700 people in the US have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.

Regaining measles elimination status requires demonstrating that measles transmission has stopped and is not sustained for 12 months, and that the country has a high-quality, functioning surveillance system.

But measles outbreaks continue to appear in places like Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin, with no clear evidence that transmission has ended nationally, said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University. She said it is unlikely that all measles cases were being counted.

In its letter, PAHO urged the US to intensify its vaccination efforts to halt transmission of the highly contagious virus, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a decision that is not yet public.

"What we need to do is terminate the current transmission. To do that, we need to enhance immunization uptake in virtually all communities," said Walter Orenstein, a professor emeritus at Emory University.

Orenstein was a member of the US independent advisory panel that presented the CDC's measles status report along with its assessment that the US had likely lost its measles elimination status to PAHO in a meeting last week.

DECLINING VACCINATION RATES, GROWING MISTRUST

Public trust in vaccination fell during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and messaging from Kennedy and the White House about the risks of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine has exacerbated those concerns, several experts said.

While the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said it supports vaccinations for measles, the government has put millions of dollars into investigating vaccine safety and publicly pushed several states to loosen school vaccine mandates.

"Regaining that trust takes time, and requires a consistent effort from the officials that are working in public health," said Josh Michaud, a public health analyst with KFF, a health policy research group.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz, who has been in the job for three months, told Reuters last week that if the US loses elimination status, the agency would not change its response.

Two shots of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective at stopping the spread of measles. WHO recommends that 95% of people receive two shots of the vaccine in order to achieve herd immunity, which can protect those unable to be vaccinated and prevent spread.

In August, the CDC reported that vaccination coverage among children in kindergarten in the 2025-26 school year was 92.4%, but in certain pockets of the United States the coverage is much lower. During the South Carolina measles outbreak earlier this year, some individual schools in Spartanburg County reported immunization rates as low as 20%.

Dr. Ben Kasstan-Dabush, assistant professor of global health & development at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said the US needs to increase vaccinations across all groups.

As part of its evaluation, PAHO reviewed epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the CDC to determine whether the same strain of measles had been circulating in the United States for 12 months or longer. The senior administration official said the outbreak in Utah, which began in June 2025, was key to PAHO's determination.

Other critical tools needed to improve the US response include improving surveillance networks to be able to identify and test for the virus and beefing up epidemiological capacity to follow up on cases and interrupt chains of transmission.

Orenstein said it is critical that the United States resume its support for global immunization efforts, which were disrupted when the US dropped out of the World Health Organization.

He said every US measles case in the past two years originated as an imported virus, often brought in by Americans traveling abroad who then sparked local outbreaks.

items.title: New York Mayor Mamdani disbands 'notorious' police unit that used excessive force on protesters
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 16 (Reuters) - New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is disbanding a police unit criticized for using excessive force against protesters in favor of a new "civilian-led approach" to large public demonstrations, he announced on Monday.

Mamdani promised in his election campaign last year to disband the police department's Strategic Response Group, a decade-old anti-terrorism unit that has faced legal challenges for its rough tactics at street protests, including the use of pepper spray by armed officers in riot gear and mass arrests.

In the joint announcement alongside New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, Mamdani said he is creating a new civilian-led group called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, whose members would be unarmed and would not have arrest powers.

At the New York Police Department, he said the disbanded SRG unit would be replaced in part by a new unit called the Patrol Support Division, which he said would police protests differently.

"New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," the mayor said in a statement.

A 'NOTORIOUS' UNIT

The SRG was rebuked in a 2023 legal settlement after New York Attorney General Letitia James, the New York Civil Liberties Union and others sued over excessive force against protesters, journalists and legal observers during protests against police violence in the summer of 2020.

The NYCLU and other civil rights groups cautiously welcomed Mamdani's announcement, while expressing concern that the new Patrol Support Division might end up a rebranding of the SRG, not a disbanding.

The Legal Aid Society, the city's largest public defender's office, on Monday commended the disbanding of "one of the NYPD's most notorious units" in a statement, but said the new unit "will require vigilant oversight to ensure that the SRG's tactics are not repeated."

The NYCLU said it will be "monitoring this new unit closely, including for compliance with our 2023 settlement with the City."

Tisch, who runs one of the world's largest police forces and its nearly $7 billion annual operating budget, said there were about 500 SRG officers who would be reassigned within the department before next spring. Some, she added, would go to the existing Counterterrorism Bureau.

"Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions," Tisch told ABC's Eyewitness News in a joint interview with the mayor.

A spokesperson for the mayor did not respond to queries about how the new Patrol Support Division would differ from the SRG, or whether it would be staffed by former SRG officers.

Police unions criticized the move, saying it would endanger the safety of officers and the public.

"The next time your life is disrupted by demonstrators who are blocking bridges and roadways or causing chaos on our streets, remember: Mayor Mamdani is on their side, not yours," Patrick Hendry, president of the Police Benevolent Association, said in a statement.

items.title: Top cases on the US Supreme Court's docket
items.content_html:
November 16 - The US Supreme Court is hearing a series of important cases during its current nine-month term involving issues such as President Donald Trump's immigration policies, asylum, assault-style rifle bans, race, Big Oil's role in climate change, Republican-backed voting restrictions, LGBT rights and more.

Here is a look at some of the cases being argued during the term, which runs to about the end of June.

BAN ON ASSAULT-STYLE RIFLES

The justices will hear arguments on December 2 in a challenge to the legality of state prohibitions on assault-style rifles, giving them another chance to expand gun rights in a case that involves a type of weapon often associated with mass shootings. Lower courts upheld bans in Cook County, Illinois, and Connecticut on powerful semiautomatic rifles such as AR-15s. The lower courts rejected arguments that the measures violate the US Constitution's Second Amendment right to "keep and bear arms." Gun rights groups and other challengers have said that Supreme Court precedents concerning the Second Amendment protect these firearms, which they have described as in "common use." A ruling is expected by the end of June.

TRUMP'S ASYLUM RESTRICTIONS

The court will decide the legality of Trump's restrictions on access to asylum at the US-Mexico border. His administration appealed after a lower court ruled that Trump exceeded his authority by denying migrants caught entering the US illegally the chance to apply for asylum. The ban also applies to migrants who arrive at official border crossings and lack certain medical or criminal history information, a requirement advocates say is often impossible to meet for people fleeing violence. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

TRUMP'S MANDATORY IMMIGRATION DETENTION

The court will decide the legality of Trump's policy that subjects millions of immigrants in the US illegally to mandatory detention during deportation proceedings. The policy is part of Trump's pursuit of mass deportation. The justices took up the Trump administration's appeal of a lower court's ruling against the policy in a case involving a Brazilian national. The administration abandoned the US government's longstanding interpretation of federal law that immigrants already living in the US could be released on bond while their cases play out in immigration court. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

TRUMP'S THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTATIONS

The justices will hear arguments in December over the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to nations other than their own — so-called "third countries" — without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face. The court on September 29 let the administration continue the policy for the time being, putting on hold a federal judge's ruling that removing migrants to third countries is unlawful. More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy, according to human rights groups. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

ASYLUM AND TERRORISM

The court will hear the Trump administration's bid to deny asylum to a man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist group in Nigeria — a case that could expand what officials may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law. The Justice Department appealed a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba. He was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be a terrorist organization. The lower court ruled that cooking did not qualify as "material support" for terrorism under the immigration statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

BIG OIL CLIMATE SUIT

The justices wrestled with complex questions over whether to let local governments try to hold oil companies liable for the harms caused by climate change during October 5 arguments in a bid by ExxonMobil (XOM.N) and Suncor Energy (SU.TO) to thwart a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colorado. The companies appealed after Colorado's top court allowed Boulder's lawsuit accusing them of violating state law and seeking unspecified monetary damages. The Trump administration backed the companies. The justices voiced concerns about unduly limiting the authority of states to pursue climate-related litigation, as well as the potential to unleash chaos if local governments across the country were permitted to sue these companies. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

VOTING RIGHTS

The justices will hear arguments on December 8 in a Republican-led bid to revive voter restrictions in Arizona that would stiffen proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registrants and purge state voter rolls of alleged non-US citizens. Republicans appealed after a lower court halted provisions of Arizona's law because they were found to violate a federal voting registration statute. President Donald Trump's administration has backed key elements of the appeal. Critics have said the Arizona measure adds extra mandates for voting that unfairly target Latino, Native American and student voters. Those groups tend to favor Democratic candidates. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

RACE IN STUDENT ADMISSIONS

The justices will consider whether to revive a lawsuit against a Maryland county's lottery admissions policy for four elite public middle schools that some parents claim unlawfully discriminates against Asian American applicants. The case has the court delving again into the contentious issue of race in student admissions. A coalition of parents appealed a lower court's decision rejecting their claim that Montgomery County's policy violates the US Constitution's 14th Amendment guarantee of equal protection under the law. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

LGBT RIGHTS

The justices will hear arguments on November 3 in a bid by the Archdiocese of Denver and other Catholic entities to be exempted from a Colorado preschool funding program's nondiscrimination requirement. A lower court found that Colorado's program did not violate the religious rights of the Catholic plaintiffs under the US Constitution's First Amendment. The program provides state funds for preschools. The Catholic plaintiffs objected to the state's requirement that schools receiving funding under the program give all children "equal opportunity" to enroll in preschool regardless of certain characteristics, including the sexual orientation or gender identity of students or their family members. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

DOGE TRANSPARENCY

The justices will decide whether the Trump administration can avoid handing over records to a watchdog group about its Department of Government Efficiency, an initiative aimed at slashing agency budgets and workers spearheaded last year by the president's former adviser Elon Musk. The administration appealed a judge's order for DOGE to respond to requests by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington for information about its operations. The judge found that DOGE likely is a government agency covered by the federal Freedom of Information Act, or FOIA. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

FEDERAL BAN ON HOME DISTILLING

The court will decide the legality of a federal ban on the home distilling of alcoholic spirits that was enacted in 1868 after the US Civil War to crack down on liquor tax evasion. The dispute pits the Trump administration, which is defending the law, against challengers who argue that the home-distilling prohibition exceeds the authority of Congress under the US Constitution. More than a dozen Republican-led states have backed the legal challenge to the statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

EPIC GAMES SUIT AGAINST APPLE

The justices will hear arguments on January 11 on Apple's (AAPL.O) bid to escape being found in contempt in its legal fight with "Fortnite" maker Epic Games after the iPhone maker was deemed in violation of a judicial order mandating sweeping changes to its lucrative App Store in the antitrust litigation. Apple appealed a lower court's ruling upholding a decision by an Oakland, California-based federal judge finding Apple in contempt in Epic's 2020 lawsuit contesting App Store fees. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

PEPSICO TRADEMARK CASE

The court will hear arguments on January 12 in a bid by canned-coffee maker Rise Brewing to hold PepsiCo (PEP.O) liable for alleged trademark infringement concerning Pepsi's morning energy drink "Mtn Dew Rise." Rise appealed a lower court's ruling rejecting the company's claim that the product name "Mtn Dew Rise" infringes its trademarks and creates customer confusion with its coffee brand. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

Compiled by Andrew Chung and John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham

items.title: Classified US national security communications network hit by outage, NSA says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The highly classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for its internal communications experienced a "temporary degradation" during scheduled maintenance, the agency said Tuesday.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," the NSA said.

CNN, which first reported on the outage, said that it affected NSANet, which allows employees to share classified information internally.

Reuters could not independently determine the extent or the length of the outage.

The incident comes amid increased concern over a series of tech problems, notably faults that snarled US air traffic and triggered a Microsoft email blackout late last week.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday played down the disruptions, saying such problems were inevitable.

"Things like that happen," Trump told reporters in Manila when asked about the outages. "It's fine."

Reporting by Daphne Psaledakis and Ismail Shakil; Editing by Caitlin Webber, Chizu Nomiyama and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: US air travel recovery stumbles on United pause as funding fight brews
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - US air travel largely returned to normal on Monday after more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days stemming from Friday's longest ground stop in 25 years, though the resumption was briefly marred by a United Airlines technology outage.

Speaking on CNBC, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy estimated the economic impact of the broader disruptions — which also delayed nearly 28,000 flights — would be in the billions of dollars. The problem was suspected to have been caused by a single router installed during routine maintenance.

United (UAL.O) on Monday experienced a technology outage affecting its departing flights for about an hour. The issue was resolved by 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT) and did not affect other airlines.

As of 6:50 p.m. ET, United had delayed 645 flights, or 20% of its schedule, and canceled 25 on Monday, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.

It was unclear how many of those disruptions were caused by Monday's technology issue, as airlines were still recovering from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop.

As air travel stabilized, the conversation in Washington turned to how the air traffic control network will be fixed, how it will be funded and who was to blame for Friday's alarming shutdown.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Monday that only $4 billion of $12.5 billion approved by Congress to improve air traffic control systems had been spent. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune said.

He said just $12 billion of the $30 billion in more funding sought last week was for air traffic modernization, with the remainder for airport-related projects.

By 6 p.m. ET on Monday there were 344 flight cancellations and 4,800 delays, down from more than 2,300 canceled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware.

The four largest US airlines could face a $345 million earnings hit from the nationwide ground stop, brokerage Bernstein estimates.

FUNDING FOR UPGRADES

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that funding was needed to upgrade the air traffic control system. "Essentially, what you saw was very old equipment that had a heart attack," Trump told reporters.

Duffy on Friday raised his request for funding for air traffic control and airports to $50 billion from $30 billion. The FAA is still using aging equipment including Compaq computers, floppy disks, 25-year-old obsolete routers and paper strips to track aircraft.

"This rickety system is telegraphing to the American people, 'Hey, we need investment'," Duffy said on Monday. "Now is the time to do a big dollar amount to modernize the system."

Republican Senator Eric Schmitt weighed in by saying the necessary funding was long overdue. "We should just go all in here and get this thing fixed," Schmitt told Reuters. "The can has been kicked for a long time ... Clearly this is a decades-old problem in the making."

Democrats in Congress say Duffy has spent or committed to spend just $4 billion of the initial $12.5 billion approved last year for air traffic control, while the Transportation Department said it had finalized plans for much of the funding and needs more money for telecoms upgrades.

"They have money, they don't use it, and then they come back and say, 'Give us more money.' Well, we want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it, and they don't," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said on Monday.

Democrats also want hearings into what led to the communications disruptions that brought nearly all US air travel to a halt for more than four hours on Friday.

Duffy and Republicans want quick action on the additional funding in the final weeks before the current Congress goes home and Democrats take over in January.

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Kevin Liffey, David Goodman and Jamie Freed
